newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Grain-Price turmoil, shipments up.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Grain-Price turmoil, shipments up.

text.p: Australian grain markets are finding their feet after being thrown into turmoil last week by an unexpectedly big estimated price increase by the Australian Wheat Board (AWB) for pooled wheat for export markets.
The trade had expected a steady pool price in the AWB's regular revision on Monday, at most a A$5.00 a tonne rise.

Instead the AWB boosted estimated pool prices for most grades by A$10.00 a tonne, taking the price for benchmark Australian Standard White (ASW) to A$185.00 a tonne. Prices for lower grade types were increased by A$20.00 a tonne while prices
for premium grades were increased by A$5.00 a tonne.
The surprise rises threw market prices into disarray.

On Tuesday, futures prices for near-term contracts shot up by about A$10.00 a tonne, while the AWB's Newcastle indicator prices jumped by A$15.00 to A$155.00 a tonne for ASW and by A$13.00 to A$191.00 for Australian Prime Hard.
Cash prices jumped by about A$10.00 a tonne.

Surprise in the trade was heightened by the fact that the pool price rise was despite a strongly rising Australian dollar, which peaked at 82.12 U.S. cents during the week, and a declining Chicago wheat futures market.

Brokers and traders saw the AWB move indicating an urgent need for wheat to meet export contracts. The AWB had no substantive comment beyond a statement by spokesman Alex Nichol that pool returns reflected the volatility of the market.

After what Bill Mitchell of New England Agricultural Traders described as "a pretty hectic week," prices settled back across the board by Friday with late-week price slumps overtaking the big gains earlier in the week.
Over the week, near-term futures contracts were up by between A$4.00 and A$9.00 a tonne, with market leader January 1997 posting the biggest gain.

The AWB's Newcastle indicator prices for ASW on balance roise by A$12.00 at A$152.00 a tonne, AH was down by A$3.00 a tonne to A$159.00 (after a suspension of quotes on Thursday), while APH was down by A$8.00 to A$171.00.

In the cash market, AH firmed A$5.00 after the pool price announcement then dropped A$10.00, ending the week at about A$140.00 Moree silo, Mitchell said. Soft wheat and ASW rose A$10.00 after the pool price rise then dropped A$10.00 to end the week steady on about A$127.00.
At the close of the week, most cash bids were about A$10.00 a tonne behind estimated pool returns. A week ago, cash prices were near pool values, "we knew what was going on," he said.
But after the week's gyrations, millers had pulled their bids back, leaving physical traders with nowhere to go. They pulled back too, he said.

The possibility of the AWB being forced to reduce its pool price now was being lessened by Chicago's rally, Mitchell and brokers pointed out on Friday. The feeling was that the AWB had a chance of getting away with what they saw as a gamble.
Brokers looked for a quiet period to mid-January.

While the week's price drama rolled on, Australia's wheat shipments continued at high levels, reaching more than a quarter of a million tonnes during the week. This brought shipments so far this year to 2.095 million tonnes against 1.470 million tonnes at the same time last year, the AWB's Nichol said.
